reference.source: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care / Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn
clinicalPearls: Intraventricular haemorrhage most often originates from the fragile germinal matrix and is predominantly a disease of preterm and very low birth weight infants
Risk is greatest in the first days of life, so routine cranial ultrasound screening is performed early and repeated in at-risk preterm infants
Severity is described by a grading system from mild germinal matrix or small intraventricular bleeds through to bleeds with ventricular dilatation and associated haemorrhagic parenchymal infarction
Presentation ranges from clinically silent to a sudden catastrophic deterioration with collapse, falling haematocrit, bulging fontanelle, and seizures
Fluctuations in cerebral blood flow, systemic blood pressure, hypercarbia, acidosis, and coagulation disturbance all contribute to bleeding from immature vessels
Post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation is an important complication requiring serial head circumference and ultrasound monitoring and sometimes cerebrospinal fluid drainage
Prevention focuses on antenatal corticosteroids, careful delivery and resuscitation, and minimising haemodynamic and respiratory instability in the early neonatal period
reference.pathophysiology: Neonatal intraventricular haemorrhage in the preterm infant arises from the germinal matrix, a highly vascular and metabolically active region near the caudate that is present until around term. Its capillaries are structurally immature and fragile, and the region has limited autoregulatory support, so it is vulnerable to rupture when cerebral blood flow or venous pressure fluctuates. Contributing factors include pressure-passive cerebral circulation, swings in arterial pressure, hypercarbia and hypoxia, coagulopathy, and rapid volume shifts. Bleeding may remain confined to the germinal matrix or rupture into the ventricular system, and when it obstructs cerebrospinal fluid flow it causes post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation. Associated venous congestion can lead to periventricular haemorrhagic infarction of the surrounding white matter, the most severe pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Periventricular leukomalacia and other white matter injury
Neonatal seizures from hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy or metabolic causes
Neonatal sepsis or meningitis causing acute deterioration
Other intracranial haemorrhage such as subdural or subarachnoid bleeding
Congenital hydrocephalus from a non-haemorrhagic cause
Coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia causing bleeding elsewhere
additionalInvestigations: Cranial ultrasound for screening, grading, and serial monitoring of ventricular size
Serial head circumference measurement to detect post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation
Full blood count and coagulation studies to identify anaemia or bleeding tendency
Blood gas and metabolic monitoring for hypercarbia, acidosis, and instability
MRI for detailed assessment of parenchymal injury and prognosis when needed
Cerebrospinal fluid assessment when infection or progressive hydrocephalus is suspected
redFlags: Acute collapse with a sudden fall in haematocrit, bulging fontanelle, and seizures
High-grade haemorrhage with ventricular dilatation or parenchymal infarction
Rapidly increasing head circumference and progressive ventricular enlargement
Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as apnoea, bradycardia, and altered consciousness
reference.prognosis: Outcome is closely linked to grade: low-grade haemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix or with minimal intraventricular blood often has a good neurodevelopmental outcome, whereas high-grade haemorrhage with ventricular dilatation or parenchymal infarction carries a substantial risk of cerebral palsy, cognitive impairment, and post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Prematurity and coexisting complications also influence long-term prognosis.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal neurological examination excludes significant haemorrhage, as many bleeds are clinically silent
Missing the early high-risk window by not screening at-risk preterm infants promptly
Overlooking gradual post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation without serial measurements
Causing haemodynamic swings through rapid boluses, aggressive ventilation, or excessive handling
Attributing deterioration to sepsis alone without considering acute haemorrhage
references: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care
management: Prioritise prevention with antenatal corticosteroids, gentle handling and avoidance of rapid swings in blood pressure, carbon dioxide and circulating volume that provoke germinal matrix bleeding
Maintain physiological stability with lung-protective ventilation to avoid hypercarbia and hypoxia, cautious fluid and inotrope use and correction of any coagulopathy
Screen and grade with routine early cranial ultrasound, repeated serially in at-risk preterm infants
Monitor for post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation with serial head circumference measurement and cranial ultrasound

Manage progressive ventricular dilatation with cerebrospinal fluid drainage via lumbar punctures or a ventricular access device, and neurosurgical referral for a ventriculoperitoneal shunt if hydrocephalus persists
Treat seizures with anticonvulsants and provide supportive neuroprotective intensive care
Arrange structured neurodevelopmental follow-up and early intervention services
